# GE Aerospace (GE) — Interrogator Forensic Dossier

*Six consecutive earnings calls: Q1 2025 (2025-04-25) → Q1 2026 (2026-04-21). Speakers: Chairman/CEO H. Lawrence "Larry" Culp; CFO Rahul Ghai; IR Blaire Shoor.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six quarters is remarkably **monotonic and self-reinforcing** — this is not a company whose thesis shifted; it is one whose thesis **compounded**. The constant through-line is the commercial-aftermarket supercycle: a ~49,000-engine (now ~80,000 total engines, ~49k commercial) installed base throwing off services revenue at ~70% of total, with "~3 out of every 4 commercial flights" running GE/CFM technology (Q2'25). Every call re-states the same three-horizon framing — "define flight for **today, tomorrow, and the future**" — and the same operating-system claim: **FLIGHT DECK**, the proprietary lean model launched ~early 2024.

What *evolved* is the magnitude and the constraint narrative, in three legible phases:

- **Phase 1 — "demand is fine, SUPPLY is the bottleneck" (Q1'25–Q2'25).** The dominant tension is the supply chain. Q1'25: total engine units **down 6%, LEAP down 13%** despite roaring orders — management blames "the slower start to material inputs in January." The story is "we cannot build/service fast enough." Simultaneously a tariff overlay appears (Q1'25: "~$500 million" net tariff cost after duty drawbacks/FTZs), then **fades almost entirely** by Q4'25 — a textbook example of a loudly-introduced risk quietly dropped once the U.S.-U.K. aerospace zero-tariff framework landed (Q2'25).

- **Phase 2 — "the supply unlock is real, raise the outlook" (Q3'25–Q4'25).** The constraint visibly breaks. Q3'25: revenue **+26%**, profit **+26%**, EPS **+44%**, LEAP deliveries **+40% YoY**, defense units **+83%**, priority-supplier material input **+35% YoY**. Q4'25: full-year orders **+32%**, the **$10B operating-profit milestone pulled forward two years** to 2026, backlog to **~$190B**. The narrative flips from apologetic ("we have a lag converting orders to revenue," Q1'25) to triumphant ("an outstanding year," Q4'25).

- **Phase 3 — "macro headwind, but the backlog is the moat" (Q1'26).** A genuinely *new* external shock enters: the Middle East/Iran conflict + elevated oil/jet fuel. Departures outlook is **cut from mid-single-digit to flat-to-low-single-digit growth**, Middle East departures down high-single-digits (Q1'26, ~5% of departures). Crucially, management does **not** cut financial guidance — it reframes: "the impact on services will likely **lag** changes in air traffic by several quarters, to be followed by a period of **above-average growth**," and de-risks the year by noting "**approximately two thirds** of the engines due for 2026 shop visits are currently off wing" and ">95% of spare parts revenue already in backlog." Orders **+87%** in Q1'26 (CES nearly doubling) is the offsetting flex.

**Growth drivers introduced/expanded over the arc:** LEAP durability kit (HPT blade, "2x time on wing," CFM56-equivalent) goes from "approved in December" (Q1'25) to "on over 30% of the LEAP-1A installed base" (Q1'26); third-party/external LEAP MRO network (XEOS Poland, MTU Dallas, Delta TechOps, Iberia as 7th Premier MRO) is built out as a *margin and capacity* lever; defense re-rates from afterthought to a second engine (orders, F-15EX/F-16 FMS, 6th-gen NGAP). **Driver quietly de-emphasized:** the tariff line item — prominent in Q1'25, essentially gone by year-end.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The financials provided **strongly corroborate** the narrative on growth and cash, with the single glaring divergence being **valuation, not execution**.

| Management claim (quarter) | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Revenue grew 11%… 26%… 29%" accelerating through the arc | Screener: FY revenue **+18.5% YoY**, 3-yr CAGR **+16.3%**; FY'25 rev $45.85B vs $38.70B FY'24 | **Corroborated.** Acceleration is real. |
| "$10B operating profit in '26, two years early" (Q4'25); EPS +44% (Q3'25) | FY'25 EPS **8.16, +36.2% YoY**; latest diluted TTM EPS 8.10; beat **7/7 quarters (100%)** | **Corroborated.** Beat-rate is perfect; profit ramp is genuine. |
| ">100% / ~130% FCF conversion" (Q3'25); "$8.0–8.4B FCF in '26" | FY FCF growth **+97.5% YoY**, FCF margin **15.8%**; **TTM FCF $7.47B** | **Corroborated** on direction. *Caveat:* TTM FCF $7.47B is the honest current run-rate, modestly below the $8.0–8.4B '26 guide — guide implies H2 weighting, consistent with Q1'26's "FCF down YoY… certain payments in Q1." |
| "Exceptional franchise… significant value creation for shareholders" | ROE **20.1%** (strong); **ROIC only 4.0%**; Net debt **$9.30B** (live-corrected — a liability, not net cash) | **Mixed.** ROE flatters; **ROIC 4% is the soft underbelly** — depressed by GE-Capital runoff/investment phase, but the per-share economics do not yet justify the price. |
| Capital returns "~$24B 2024–26… ≥70% of FCF thereafter"; $20B buyback auth (Dec'25); div +30.6% | Consistent with $7.6B repurchased in '25; balance sheet carries **$9.3B net debt** (not a fortress) | **Corroborated but levered.** Returns are real and being funded partly while net-debt-positive. |

**Where the story is RICHER than the trajectory justifies:** the **price**, not the operations. At **$335 vs Buffett FV $154** (MoS **−54%**), **P/FCF 49.3x**, and **every per-method MoS deeply negative** (DCF −100%, EPV −100%, OwnerEarnings −98%, IV15 −95%, Graham −40%), the market has fully capitalized the supercycle *and then some*. Margin is **1.50σ above its own historical peak** — i.e., the company is being valued on a margin structure at the top of its own range. Revenue momentum is the *only* metric flashing green on valuation. The narrative is impeccable; the **entry price embeds flawless multi-year execution**.

**Where the story is POORER than the numbers:** essentially nowhere on fundamentals — management has, if anything, *under-promised* (sandbagged) relative to the 7/7 beat rate. The poverty is entirely on the **margin-of-safety** axis.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: RISING, then defensively-resilient (never breaking).**

- **Q1'25 — guardedly confident, tariff-defensive.** "Operating from a position of strength" but hedged: "we're taking a more cautious approach and embedding a slower second half… departures up low single digits." Tariffs dominate Q&A.
- **Q2'25 — confident, outlook-raising.** Services outlook lifted "$4 billion… from March of last year," growth expectation moved "from high single-digit… to double-digit." Culp: "we think we're well positioned to deliver significant value creation."
- **Q3'25 — peak offensive confidence.** "Raising our full year guidance **across the board**"; "exceptional franchise with enduring competitive strengths." The supply-chain question is answered with a swagger: "It's that simple, ain't that hard."
- **Q4'25 — triumphant but disciplined.** "2025 was an outstanding year"; $10B milestone pulled forward. Still careful on margins ("flattish in 2026… feel good about trajectory").
- **Q1'26 — confident-but-cautious, macro-defensive.** New language: "embracing today's reality," "assessed multiple scenarios," "conservative… prudent, whatever words you want to use." Yet the confidence *holds*: "had it not been for the environment… we would have **raised** our guidance," and "trending toward the **high end** of that range."

**Offensive → defensive shift?** Only at the margin and only in Q1'26, and it is **macro-imposed (oil/Iran), not company-specific**. There is no shift to internal "efficiency/cost-cutting" defensiveness — the defensive language is entirely about an exogenous demand wobble that management explicitly frames as *deferred, not destroyed* demand ("Demand tends to get pushed out as opposed to going missing indefinitely," Q1'26). Specificity of guidance **increased** over the arc (segment-level margin bridges, shop-visit ranges 2,300–2,400, departure scenarios).

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: HIGH.**

This is the strongest section of the dossier. The screener records **beat 7/7 quarters (100%)**, and the transcripts show a consistent pattern of **guiding conservatively then raising**:
- Q2'25 raised the multi-year services outlook by $4B; Q3'25 raised full-year guidance "across the board" and lifted LEAP delivery growth from "15–20%" to ">20%"; Q4'25 **pulled the $10B operating-profit milestone forward by two years**.
- LEAP delivery guidance was serially beaten: "15–20%" (Q1'25) → ">20%" (Q3'25) → actual **+28%, 1,800+ units** (Q4'25).
- Q1'26: when a real shock hit, they **held** guidance rather than cutting, and called themselves "**trending toward the high end**" — and Ghai disclosed Q1 came in "**about $300 million better than what we had expected**."

**Sandbagging pattern: YES, mild and consistent** — management sets reachable bars (the "embedding a slower second half" framing in Q1'25, "conservative assumptions… between now and Labor Day" in Q1'26) and then clears them. This is the *good* kind of sandbagging (Culp's Danaher-bred lean discipline). The only credibility watch-item is that the FY'26 FCF guide ($8.0–8.4B) sits **above** the current TTM FCF ($7.47B), so the back-half must deliver — but given the 7/7 record, the burden of proof is on the skeptic.

---

- **The aftermarket-vs-ASK decoupling (recurring, Q3'25 & Q1'26).** Scott Mikus (Melius) twice pressed: aftermarket revenue is *re-accelerating* while air-traffic/ASK growth *decelerates* — "has anything structurally changed?" Management's answer (pent-up shop visits below 2019 levels, heavier wide-body work scopes, LEAP external-channel growth, price) is **plausible but is the crux of the bear case**: if the decoupling is pent-up-demand catch-up rather than structural, it normalizes. No instance in these calls of a deflected question later turning into bad news — the deflections are all on *quantification of upside*, not concealment of downside.

---

# Forensic Dossier — GE Aerospace (GE)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from five consecutive GE Aerospace earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q4 2025) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these five quarters is remarkably consistent, and that consistency is itself the headline. This is no longer the old multi-business General Electric — by the start of 2025 GE had finished breaking itself into three companies, and what remains under the "GE" ticker is GE Aerospace: a focused maker of commercial and military jet engines plus the very profitable business of servicing those engines for decades after they are sold (the "aftermarket").

Management tells one story and keeps telling it: an enormous, growing backlog of orders (rising from roughly $170 billion in early 2025 to about $190 billion by year-end), a supply chain that is slowly but steadily unclogging, and a lean operating system they call "FLIGHT DECK" that they credit for the improvement. The emphasis shifts only in degree. Early 2025 calls spend real energy on defense (tariffs, rare earths, foreign military sales) and on managing expectations down ("embedding a slower second half"). By the third and fourth quarters of 2025 the tone turns almost purely offensive: revenue up 26% in the third quarter, orders up 74% in the fourth, guidance raised "across the board," and the $10 billion operating-profit milestone pulled forward two years earlier than the original spin-off plan.

The growth drivers introduced and then leaned on harder over time are: (1) the aftermarket decoupling from air-travel growth — services revenue kept accelerating even as departures (flights flown) decelerated, because older engines (the CFM56) are staying in service longer and getting more expensive overhauls; (2) the LEAP engine fleet, expected to roughly triple by 2030, becoming a self-funding service annuity; and (3) defense output finally inflecting (units up over 80% year-over-year in the back half of 2025). Nothing was quietly dropped — the narrative widened and grew more confident, not narrower.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The unusual thing here is that the financials are *richer* than even a confident management would normally claim. The numbers corroborate the story.

| Management claim (quarter) | The hard financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Revenue grew 26%... profit up 26%" (Q3 2025); "Revenue increased 21%" full-year (Q4 2025) | Screener: revenue +18.5% year-over-year, 3-year compound growth +16.3% | Matches and arguably understates — the live figure is strong |
| "EPS... up 44%" (Q3 2025); full-year EPS strength | Screener: EPS 8.16, +36% year-over-year; but note the most recent quarter's EPS was *down ~1%* year-over-year, and trailing-twelve-month EPS is 8.10 | Mostly matches; the very latest quarter shows the growth rate cooling |
| "Free cash flow... over 130% conversion" (Q3 2025); "$8.0–8.4 billion FCF" guide for 2026 | Screener: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow $7.46 billion, up sharply year-over-year | Matches; cash generation is real and high-quality |
| "$190 billion backlog... up nearly $20 billion" (Q4 2025) | Not directly in the financials, but consistent with the 30%+ order growth reported | Credible |
| Margins "flattish" in 2026, ~21% segment level | Screener: gross margin 36.8% (stable), net margin 19.0%, both sector-leading | Matches; margins are high and steady |

Where the story is *poorer* than the price: returns and valuation. Return on invested capital (ROIC) sits at just 4.0% in the screener — strikingly low for a business management describes as an "exceptional franchise." Return on equity is a healthier 20.1%, and the gap tells you the balance sheet still carries heavy intangible and goodwill weight from the old GE. More importantly, the stock trades at about 54 times free cash flow with a recomputed net *debt* of $9.3 billion. Every one of the screener's intrinsic-value methods — discounted cash flow, earnings power, owner earnings — flags the stock as worth far less than its ~$369 price, with margins of safety of roughly negative 60% to negative 100%. The business is excellent; the price already assumes it stays excellent for a very long time.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Rising — and now near its ceiling.**

- Q1 2025: cautious-confident. Culp talks of "operating from a position of strength" but deliberately "embedding a slower second half" and quantifying tariff costs at roughly $500 million. Defensive vocabulary (tariffs, duty drawbacks, foreign trade zones) is prominent.
- Q2 2025: confident, with grace — the call is reshaped around the Air India tragedy, but management still *raises* the outlook and gives a 2028 framework.
- Q3 2025: clearly offensive. "Operational momentum is building, leading to significant growth"; guidance raised "across the board"; LEAP delivery growth bumped above 20%.
- Q4 2025 / full year: peak confidence. "2025 was an outstanding year"; the $10 billion profit target hit two years early; orders up 74% in the quarter.

The shift from defensive (tariffs, macro caution) to offensive (ramp, backlog, capacity expansion) language is real and steady. Management never over-promises on the one genuine sore spot — LEAP engine turnaround times — repeatedly saying "we know there's more to do," which reads as credible rather than evasive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is the dossier's strongest green flag. The screener records a beat in 7 of the last 7 quarters (100%). Across these calls, management set conservative full-year departure assumptions early in 2025, then raised total guidance in three consecutive quarters as the supply chain delivered. They pulled the $10 billion operating-profit milestone forward by two years and beat their own October 2025 margin assumption by about 70 basis points. There is a mild sandbagging pattern — the early-2025 "slower second half" caution proved too conservative — which is the good kind of guidance discipline. The only caution: a 100% beat rate with the stock at 54x free cash flow means perfection is now the baseline expectation, so the *bar* is the risk, not management's honesty.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring, unresolved analyst worry is **the decoupling of aftermarket growth from actual flying.** Scott Mikus (Melius) asked it twice — in Q1 and again in Q3 2025 — essentially: services revenue keeps accelerating while departures and available-seat-kilometers decelerate; what happens when the pent-up demand normalizes? Management's answer (pent-up shop visits, heavier work scopes, growth of the third-party LEAP service channel, annual price increases) is plausible but is fundamentally an argument that a cyclical surge is structural. Noah Poponak (Goldman) pushed the same point — "can you quantify the duration of the pent-up demand?" — and Culp candidly admitted "it's a hard question to answer quantitatively." That honesty is reassuring, but it leaves the single most important valuation question unanswered: how much of today's record aftermarket margin is durable versus a post-pandemic catch-up that eventually fades.

A second pressure point is **CES segment margin**, which analysts (Kahyaoglu, Seifman) repeatedly model as *flat* in 2026 despite strong revenue — the mix shift toward new-engine sales (lower margin) and the GE9X ramp are real headwinds management does not deny.

🟢 100% earnings-beat rate over seven quarters; guidance raised three quarters running.
🟢 Roughly $190 billion backlog providing multi-year revenue visibility; the company is "sold out" on LEAP and GEnx through the end of the decade.
🟢 ~70% of revenue is recurring, high-margin services — a genuine annuity tied to an installed base of ~80,000 engines.
🟢 Free-cash-flow conversion above 100%, sector-leading margins, and a credible lean operating model.

🔴 Valuation: ~54x free cash flow, trading at about 92% of its 52-week range and ~20% above its 200-day average; every intrinsic model shows a deeply negative margin of safety.
🔴 The most recent quarter's EPS was *down ~1%* year-over-year and trailing-twelve-month EPS (8.10) sits just below the reported annual figure — the growth *rate* is cooling off a very high base.
🔴 Insider behavior is one-sided: zero open-market buys against six sells (about 38,000 shares). No insider is putting fresh capital in at this price.
🔴 Analyst target velocity is *negative* (-3% versus a year ago) and the consensus target (~$380) implies only ~3% upside — the street has stopped chasing.
🔴 ROIC of 4.0% is low in absolute terms; the durable-aftermarket thesis is partly a bet that a post-pandemic catch-up is permanent.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling subtle shift is organizational. In the Q4 2025 call management folded its new "technology and operations" team into the commercial segment and elevated the customer-facing organization to report directly to the CEO — a sign they are hard-wiring the supply-chain fix into the permanent structure rather than treating it as a one-time project. They also flagged that 2026 first-quarter free cash flow will be "down year over year" because of "certain payments" — a small but real near-term cash-timing wrinkle buried in the prepared remarks.

Terminology around the aftermarket has subtly hardened from "pent-up demand" (a temporary surge) early in 2025 toward "structural" growth language (installed-base annuity, external service channel scaling to 30% by 2030) later — management is increasingly inviting investors to capitalize the surge as if it were permanent, which is precisely the assumption the valuation rests on.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.** The business is firing on every cylinder management controls — backlog, margins, cash conversion, guidance credibility — and the trajectory is genuinely improving, not merely stable.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position: this is a great company at a demanding price, not a mispricing.** The forensic work *confirms* the bull narrative; it does not uncover a hidden discount. At roughly 54x free cash flow with every intrinsic model deeply negative, insiders selling, and the analyst community's price target implying almost no upside, the entire return depends on the post-pandemic aftermarket surge proving permanent and growth not decelerating from an already-cooling base. There is no special-situation catalyst here — only the continuation of an excellent, fully-priced operating story.

On the economic moat: GE Aerospace has a **wide** moat of the intangible-plus-switching-cost type. Once an engine is certified on an airframe and an airline's fleet, the manufacturer captures decades of mandated, high-margin service revenue — a near-unbreakable installed-base annuity, with commercial aviation effectively a duopoly/triopoly (GE/CFM, Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce). Margins are high and *stable* and the backlog is widening, so the moat is intact and arguably widening on an absolute-dollar basis. The one blemish is the low reported ROIC, which reflects legacy balance-sheet weight rather than competitive erosion. No secular force threatens the terminal value: aviation is structurally growing, and the engine duopoly is one of the most durable franchises in industrials. The cheapness signal is therefore *absent* — this is the opposite of a value trap, but it is also not cheap. The risk is valuation, not moat decay.

The proprietary lean operating system they call "FLIGHT DECK" is the repeated mechanism: go to the factory floor, fix a bottleneck, lift output.

What *grows* over the six quarters is the scale of the ambition, not its direction. The backlog climbs from "$170 billion-plus" (first quarter 2025) to "roughly $175 billion" (mid-2025) to "roughly $190 billion" (fourth quarter 2025) to "over $170 billion in commercial services alone" plus more (first quarter 2026). LEAP — the newest narrow-body engine, built in a 50/50 joint venture with France's Safran — moves from a delivery-ramp story to a *durability and aftermarket-profit* story as the upgraded high-pressure-turbine blade rolls out.

The one genuinely new thread introduced late is macro caution. Tariffs appear in the first quarter of 2025 (a roughly $500 million estimated cost, largely offset). By the first quarter of 2026 a Middle East conflict and a jet-fuel/oil spike force management to cut the full-year departures assumption from mid-single-digit growth to "flat to low single-digit." | Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|

The uncomfortable counterweight is the 4.0% return on invested capital — a wide-moat business should out-earn its cost of capital, and on invested capital GE does not yet, because of the inherited goodwill base and ramp capital. bull_thesis:
GE Aerospace is one of the best businesses in the industrial world, and the operating case for it is not in dispute. It is under wing on three of every four commercial flights, has roughly 80,000 engines in service, powers two thirds of US military combat and helicopter fleets, and shares the narrow-body market with its own joint-venture partner Safran in a duopoly against RTX's Pratt & Whitney. About 70% of revenue is recurring services. The economics are the cleanest kind of annuity: an airline picking an engine makes a 25-to-30-year decision, the engine is sold cheap, and the money is earned over decades of mandatory, safety-regulated, single-source maintenance. The 2026 order wins are not this year's revenue -- they are the 2035-2055 cash flow being locked in now (American committed to more than 300 LEAP-1A engines with options for 200 more; United selected 300 GE9X engines, making it the largest GE9X operator globally; Delta committed to 60 GE9X with options for 60 more, all in the first quarter of 2026 alone).

The delivery record backs the story. Revenue grew about 18.5% over the past year and has compounded at roughly 16% over three years. Operating profit went from $8.4B to a guided $10.55-10.75B in two years. Management set a 2028 target of roughly 21% margins and hit it in 2025 -- three years early -- and set a $10B profit milestone for 2028 and hit it in 2026, two years early. Free cash flow in the second quarter of 2026 was $3.0B, up 43%, and the full-year guide was lifted to $8.9-9.2B with conversion above 100% of profit. The company has beaten expectations in eight consecutive quarters, most recently on July 16, 2026 ($2.02 adjusted per share against $1.86 expected).

The operational bear case of early 2025 is simply gone. Spare-parts delinquency and engine shortfalls dominated the first-quarter 2025 call ('total engine units were down 6% with LEAP down 13%'). By the first quarter of 2026, priority-supplier material input was up over 40% year on year, suppliers were shipping more than 95% of committed volume for three straight quarters, total engine deliveries were up 43% and commercial services revenue was up 39%. Whatever one thinks of the price, that inflection is real.

The most durable bull plank is externally verifiable and does not depend on management's word: the CFM56 fleet, the engine a naive model would treat as a melting ice cube, is retiring more slowly than planned -- 1.6% in 2025 against a 2-3% guide -- with shop visits holding at 2,300-2,400 a year through 2028 and 'no big decline come 2030.' Two thirds of that fleet has not yet had a second shop visit. Lessors renewing leases at 90-95% versus 30-40% a few years ago corroborates it from outside the company. Longer-lived CFM56s mean more shop visits, heavier work scopes and a bigger spare-parts base than anyone underwrote at the spin.

For the bull case to pay from $345.73, three conditions must hold: (1) the aftermarket boom is structural rather than a catch-up, so commercial services keeps growing well ahead of departures once pent-up demand is worked off; (2) management beats the $11.5B 2028 operating-profit target it says it could 'potentially do better' than, reaching roughly $12B; and (3) the market keeps paying today's multiple -- about 35 times operating profit and 40 times free cash flow -- on those larger 2028 numbers. All three holding produces roughly $395 a share on an 18-to-24-month view. Note what that requires: the entire return comes from earnings compounding, with zero multiple expansion. There is no valuation cushion in this thesis at all.
bear_thesis:
The bear case has nothing to do with the quality of the business and everything to do with what is being paid for it and when the bill arrives.

Start with the price. At $345.73 the market capitalisation is about $361B against guided 2026 free cash flow of $8.9-9.2B and a raised earnings guide of $7.65-7.85 a share. That is roughly 40 times free cash flow and about 45 times earnings for a company guiding to roughly 15% earnings growth. Premium engine and aerospace-systems peers -- RTX, Safran, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell -- typically trade at 25-35 times free cash flow. GE deserves the top of that band and arguably a little beyond it; it is trading above it. Meanwhile every intrinsic-value model our screener runs comes back negative: discounted cash flow fair value of $80, Buffett-style fair value of $154, and no margin of safety on any of the five methods. Those models are too harsh in isolation -- they systematically undervalue annuity franchises -- but five out of five pointing the same way is a signal about where the price sits in its own history, not noise.

Second, and more concretely: management has already told you a soft patch is coming and has told you when. On the April 21, 2026 call, the departures outlook was cut from mid-single-digit growth to 'flat to low single-digit growth', including 'a low double-digit decline in the Middle East for the year.' Culp then supplied the framework himself: 'Based on our experience during the global financial crisis, the impact on services will likely lag changes in air traffic demand by several quarters, to be followed by a period of above-average growth.' Read only the first half of that sentence. The traffic hit is dated to roughly 2027 -- outside every number management has guided. The reason 2026 is safe is stated plainly: 'approximately two thirds of the engines due for our projected shop visits for all of 2026 are currently off wing.' The engines already in the shop cannot un-fly. But that is exactly why 2026 tells you nothing about 2027: next year's shop visits are today's flights, on routes whose fuel economics just changed (US airlines spent $6.66B on jet fuel in May 2026, up 84% year on year).

Third, the load-bearing question of the entire story is one management will not answer. Noah Poponak of Goldman Sachs asked in the second quarter of 2025 to 'quantify the duration of the pent-up demand.' Culp: 'Well, it's a hard question to answer quantitatively.' Scott Mikus of Melius asked in the third quarter of 2025 whether anything structural lets aftermarket growth outrun traffic growth permanently. Ghai's answer named three drivers: 'It's pent-up demand, work scopes and then growth of external channel.' Two of those three are explicitly temporary. Commercial services grew 39% in the first quarter of 2026 while departures grew low single digits -- that gap is a catch-up, and catch-ups close. At 45 times earnings you are paying for the gap as though it were permanent, at the precise moment the two people who run it decline to size it.

Fourth, margin expansion is on hold by management's own account. Commercial Engines & Services margins are guided flat for 2026 despite roughly $3.5B of incremental services revenue, because new-engine sales are outgrowing services and the GE9X is sold at a loss that 'should also peak by the time we get to 2028.' So the next two years offer volume growth, not margin growth -- and the multiple is priced as though it were both.

Fifth, the beat is fully capitalised. Eight consecutive beats and serial raises mean the market has learned this team sandbags -- Ghai admitted it in April 2026: 'had it not been for the environment that we are in... we would have raised our guidance. The first quarter was about $300 million better than what we had expected.' A 100% beat rate is not an edge; it is an expectation. The proof arrived on July 16, 2026: a 9% earnings beat and a roughly 7% raise to the full-year midpoint, and the stock fell about 4% -- the second consecutive negative reaction to good news. When beat-and-raise stops paying, the multiple is the whole trade.

What would confirm the bear case: a 2027 guide at the January 2027 print that shows the departures lag arriving in shop-visit volumes; commercial services growth converging toward departures growth; any evidence the third-party repair channel is taking spare-parts share rather than adding it; or Boeing's public complaint about GEnx delivery delays (Reuters, July 16, 2026 -- Culp pushed back) turning into a share or penalty issue. Also watch the corroborating tells already in hand: insiders have made zero open-market purchases against six sales totalling 38,198 shares, and management is reinvesting all $8-9B of free cash flow into the ramp rather than buying stock -- so there is no mechanical support under the shares at 45 times earnings. Note what is NOT in the bear case: there is no solvency issue (net debt of $9.81B against roughly $9B of annual free cash flow; Altman-Z of 3.7), no secular threat, and no accounting problem. This is a great company at a bad price, which is a different and slower risk than a bad company.

We do not disagree with Wall Street about this company. We disagree about the price, and specifically about one number nobody is modelling.

The street's consensus target is $406.57, with a median of $400, a high of $455 (Sheila Kahyaoglu, July 2, 2026, when the stock was $380.41) and a low of $374. He got the raise. The stock then fell 4%. That is the entire consensus problem in one sequence: the street is forecasting the beat correctly and mis-forecasting the reaction, because the beat is already in the price.

The specific street assumption that is wrong is this: consensus carries GE's aftermarket at a permanent, bond-like growth premium -- roughly 45 times forward earnings and 40 times free cash flow -- while embedding no scenario in which the departures downgrade of April 21, 2026 (cut from mid-single-digit growth to flat-to-low-single-digit, with the Middle East down low double digits) transmits into 2027 shop-visit volumes. The street is extrapolating a year that management has explicitly told it is pre-loaded.

The second wrong assumption is that commercial services growth of 39% against low-single-digit departure growth (first quarter of 2026) is a structural decoupling. We are not making a contrarian call on GE Aerospace. We are declining to pay 40 times free cash flow for it.

The regime we are trading in makes that worse, not better: a hawkish Fed with hike odds near 77% by December, no strategist assuming any multiple expansion, and a dispersion tape where single names re-rate violently on events. interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — GE Aerospace (GE)
**Prepared:** 2026-07-17 · **Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (Apr 25, 2025) · Q2 2025 + Investor Update (Jul 17, 2025) · Q3 2025 (Oct 21, 2025) · Q4/FY 2025 (Jan 22, 2026) · Q1 2026 (Apr 21, 2026) · **Live price used:** $345.73 (US dollars, NYSE, 2026-07-17)

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has moved through three distinct phases in five quarters, and the direction of travel is unambiguously upward — which is precisely why the setup deserves scrutiny.

**Phase one — "we are supply-constrained, please be patient" (Q1 2025).** The opening call is defensive in structure even though the numbers were good. Larry Culp led with tariffs ("we expect to reduce the tariff costs to roughly $500 million"), with a cautious cut to the departures assumption ("we're taking a more cautious approach and embedding a slower second half"), and with an admission that revenue was being held back by the company's own supply chain: "our spare parts delinquency continues to increase, unfortunately, up over 2x year-over-year," and "total engine units were down 6% with LEAP down 13%." The hero of the story was FLIGHT DECK, the company's in-house lean operating system, and the ask was time.

**Phase two — "the constraint is breaking, and the ceiling is higher than we said" (Q2 2025 through Q4 2025).** At the July 2025 Investor Update the framing flipped from patience to ambition. Management raised the multi-year services outlook by roughly $4 billion versus its March 2024 view — Rahul Ghai: "we went from high single-digit growth expectation to a double-digit growth expectation... coming off a higher starting point" — and introduced a 2028 target of $11.5 billion in operating profit. New drivers were introduced that had not been part of the original spin-off pitch, and they are the most important part of the arc: **fewer CFM56 retirements than modelled** (600 incremental shop visits pulled into the 2028 window because "these fleets are just continuing to fly longer"), **heavier work scopes** on maturing wide-body engines, and **growth of the third-party repair channel**. By Q3 2025 the tone was frankly triumphant — revenue up 26%, defense units up 83%, LEAP delivery growth raised from "15% to 20%" to "more than 20%." By Q4 2025 Culp was able to say the company would hit its $10 billion profit milestone "two years earlier than our outlook has been."

**Phase three — "a macro shock arrived and we are absorbing it" (Q1 2026 to today).** The April 2026 call opens with the Middle East conflict. Departures guidance was cut from mid-single-digit growth to "flat to low single-digit growth," including "a low double-digit decline in the Middle East for the year." But — and this is the pivotal manoeuvre of the whole arc — management simultaneously **held full-year guidance and said it was trending to the high end**, and pre-installed an explanatory framework for why the traffic hit would not show up in the numbers now: "Based on our experience during the global financial crisis, the impact on services will likely lag changes in air traffic demand by several quarters, to be followed by a period of above-average growth."

**Nothing has been quietly dropped.** Every driver introduced has been reaffirmed or raised. That is rare and it is genuinely to management's credit. What has changed is the *nature of the risk*: it moved from an operational problem the company controls (supply chain) to a demand problem it does not (air traffic, jet fuel, geopolitics) — and management's own words locate the arrival of that risk several quarters out, not now.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where / when | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "GE Aerospace is an exceptional franchise" with double-digit growth | Every call | Revenue +18.5% year on year, three-year compound rate +16.3%; 2023 $35.35B → 2025 $45.85B | **Corroborated.** Not a narrative — an arithmetic fact. |
| $10 billion of operating profit is achievable "two years earlier than our outlook" | Q4 2025 (Jan 2026) | 2026 guidance now $10.55–10.75B after the July 16, 2026 raise | **Over-delivered.** They beat their own accelerated milestone. |
| "Back in July when we gave 2028 guidance, expected around 21% margins in '28. We got there last year." | Q4 2025 | Gross margin 36.8% and stable; net margin 19.0%, best-in-class among engine peers | **Corroborated, and it is the single most impressive fact in the file.** A three-year margin target hit in year one. |
| Robust demand; backlog growing | Q1 2025 → Q1 2026 | Backlog $170B (Q1 2025) → $175B (Q2/Q3 2025) → ~$190B (Q4 2025); commercial services backlog >$140B → >$170B | **Corroborated and accelerating.** |
| Free cash flow conversion "well above 100%" | Q4 2025, Q1 2026 | Reported Q2 2026 free cash flow $3.0B, up 43%; full-year guide raised to $8.9–9.2B | **Corroborated by the reported figures.** ⚠️ **Data integrity flag:** our screener's trailing-twelve-month free-cash-flow field reads $3.59B, which cannot be reconciled with a single quarter of $3.0B or a $8.9–9.2B annual guide. The screener field is unreliable here; the company-reported and guided figures are the ones to underwrite. The 52.9x price-to-free-cash-flow in the scan is therefore also mis-stated — the honest figure on 2026 guidance is roughly **40x**, which is still expensive, just not absurd. |
| CFM56 "flying longer," retirements below plan | Q4 2025, Q1 2026 | Retirements 1.6% in 2025 versus a 2–3% guide; shop visits 2,300–2,400 per year through 2028; "about two thirds of the fleet has yet to undergo a second shop visit" (Q1 2026) | **Corroborated by an external, checkable fact** (lessors renewing leases at 90–95% versus 30–40% previously). This is the highest-quality plank of the bull case. |
| Earnings beats are routine | — | Beat in 7 of 7 quarters in the scan; the July 16, 2026 print made it 8 of 8 ($2.02 adjusted versus $1.86 expected) | **Corroborated — and this is a warning, not only a compliment.** A 100% beat rate means the beat is in the price. |
| Returns are strong | — | Return on equity 20.1% — but the scan's return on invested capital reads **4.0%** | **Divergent, and the divergence is mostly an accounting artifact.** GE's post-spin balance sheet still carries substantial goodwill and intangibles from the old conglomerate; the invested-capital denominator flatters nobody. The economic reality — a company earning ~$10.6B of operating profit on a franchise whose incremental capital needs are ~$1B a year of US plant plus ~$3B of R&D — is a very high-return business. But the 4.0% figure means **you cannot use returns on capital to argue this moat is widening; you have to use margins and profit growth, which do support it.** |
| Book value | — | Book value per share compounding at **−16.9% over five years** | **Divergent but explicable.** This is the spin-off of GE HealthCare and GE Vernova plus buybacks, not value destruction. | Tariffs manageable at ~$500M | Q1 2025 | No tariff blow-up has appeared in any subsequent margin line | **Corroborated so far.** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify:** nowhere on the operating line. The place the narrative outruns the evidence is on **margin durability inside Commercial Engines & Services**. Management guides that segment's 2026 margins to be *flat* despite roughly $3.5 billion of incremental services revenue dropping through at a healthy rate. The reason is honest and stated — new-engine sales are growing faster than services, and the GE9X wide-body engine is being sold at a loss that management concedes will not peak until 2028. So the profit growth on offer for the next two years is a **volume** story, not a **margin-expansion** story, and the current valuation is being paid as though it were both.

**Where the story is poorer than the numbers justify:** the free-cash-flow guide. Free cash flow up 43% in a quarter, with a raise to $8.9–9.2 billion, against a company that a year ago was fighting a billion-dollar inventory build, is being under-narrated. Ghai's Q4 2025 line — "nothing abnormal coming into the cash number and more opportunity on inventory as we get out" — is understated relative to what actually printed.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, then deliberately re-anchored to caution — and the caution is the informative part.**

| Quarter | Posture | Quoted evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | **Defensive-operational.** Apologetic about output. | "Our spare parts delinquency continues to increase, unfortunately, up over 2x year-over-year." · "Total engine units were down 6% with LEAP down 13%." · "The broader environment is certainly uncertain." |
| Q2 2025 | **Offensive.** Raised the multi-year ceiling and put a 2028 number on the table. | "We think GE Aerospace is an exceptional franchise with real tremendous competitive advantages." · Services outlook raised ~$4B. |
| Q3 2025 | **Confident-operational.** The proof arrived. | "Our exceptional third quarter and year-to-date results demonstrate FLIGHT DECK in action." · "Operational momentum is building." |
| Q4 2025 | **Peak confidence.** Milestones pulled forward. | "$10 billion of profit in '26, two years earlier than our outlook has been." · "Potentially do better" than the $11.5B 2028 target. |
| Q1 2026 | **Confident-but-hedging.** Growth language intact, macro language inserted. | "Orders were up 87%." · But: "We are reducing our full-year departures outlook from mid-single-digit growth to flat to low single-digit growth." · "The second half is just about what we do not know. Hopefully... we are being conservative and cautious — prudent, whatever words you want to use." |

**The shift from offense to defense is real but narrow.** Management did not become defensive about the *business*; it became defensive about *the tape it cannot control*. Culp's Q1 2026 answer to Seth Seifman on jet fuel is the tell: "I hope what we are taking is a conservative set of assumptions on board here between now and, let us say, Labor Day. Time will tell." That is a CEO buying himself optionality on the second half — and, as of the July 16, 2026 print, it worked exactly as intended.

**Specificity of guidance has gone up, not down**, over the five quarters: from a maintained range in April 2025, to a dated 2028 framework in July 2025, to shop-visit counts (2,300–2,400), retirement percentages (1.6% actual versus 2–3% guided), and durability-kit penetration (">30% of the LEAP-1A installed base") by 2026. Companies in trouble get vaguer. This one got more granular. That is a strong credibility signal.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High.** This is, on the evidence in front of me, one of the more reliable guidance records in large-cap industrials.

Track the promises forward:

1. **Q1 2025 promise:** maintain full-year guidance despite ~$500M of tariff cost and a cut to departures. **Delivered** — Q3 2025 raised guidance "across the board."
2. **Q1 2025 promise:** "15% to 20% growth in LEAP deliveries we expect in 2025." **Over-delivered** — raised to "more than 20%" in Q3 2025; the full year printed LEAP units up 28%, exceeding 1,800, a program record.
3. **July 2025 promise:** ~21% margins by 2028. **Over-delivered by three years** — "We got there last year" (Q4 2025).
4. **July 2025 promise:** $10B of operating profit by 2028. **Over-delivered by two years** — hit at the 2026 guidance midpoint.
5. **Jan 2026 guide:** operating profit $9.85–10.25B, adjusted earnings per share $7.10–7.40, free cash flow $8.0–8.4B. **Raised twice within six months** — to $10.55–10.75B, $7.65–7.85, and $8.9–9.2B on July 16, 2026.
6. **Q1 2026 promise:** holding full-year guidance despite the departures cut, "trending toward the high end." **Delivered and then some** — the July 16 raise went above the old high end.

**Sandbagging pattern: confirmed, and management effectively admitted it.** Ghai, Q1 2026: "had it not been for the environment that we are in... **we would have raised our guidance**. The first quarter was about $300 million better than what we had expected at the beginning of the year." That is a CFO telling you the number is conservative and holding the beat in reserve. Three months later he spent it.

**The investment consequence of a High score is counter-intuitive.** An 8-for-8 beat rate with serial raises does not create an opportunity — it *removes* one. There is no expectations gap left to arbitrage. The market has learned this management sandbags, and prices the sandbag. That is why the stock fell about 4% on a quarter that beat by 9% and raised the full year by roughly 7% at the midpoint.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The one question management cannot answer, and analysts keep asking: how much of the aftermarket boom is structural versus pent-up?**

Noah Poponak (Goldman Sachs) asked it directly in Q2 2025: "I wonder if you can quantify the duration of the pent-up demand? Will it take you 1, 2, 3 years to get through that?" Culp's answer: **"Well, it's a hard question to answer quantitatively."** He then redirected to the backlog. Scott Mikus (Melius) asked the same thing from the other side in Q3 2025 — "has anything structurally changed about the business model that could cause your aftermarket growth to decouple or sustainably outperform [available-seat-kilometre] growth over the long-term?" — and Ghai's answer named three things, two of which are explicitly temporary: **"It's pent-up demand, work scopes and then growth of external channel."**

This is the load-bearing unanswered question in the entire file. Commercial services revenue grew 39% in Q1 2026 while global departures grew low single digits. That gap is not a permanent feature of physics; it is a catch-up. Management will not size it, because sizing it would let the market model the year it closes.

**The margin question, asked every single quarter, and never fully resolved.** Sheila Kahyaoglu (Jefferies) in Q4 2025: margins at the midpoint "imply margins are flat" — walk me through it. Seth Seifman (JPMorgan) the same call: "the headwinds accumulating from a mix perspective." The answer is consistent and honest (new-engine mix, GE9X losses through 2028) but the conclusion analysts keep circling is that **profit growth is coming from volume, and volume is coming from a supply chain that is fixing itself — a one-time unlock, not a compounding one.**

**Topics analysts pushed on that later turned into news:** the tariff line (Q1 2025) has so far been a non-event. But **Robert Stallard's (Vertical Research) Q3 2025 durability question** — "how long is it going to take to roll that blade out across the installed base?" — got the answer "it's probably a multiyear effort," and by Q1 2026 the durability kit was on only ">30% of the LEAP-1A installed base." A multi-year fleet retrofit is a multi-year cost and a multi-year customer-goodwill liability.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** the price. Nobody on any of these five calls asked why a business guiding to ~15% earnings growth should trade at ~45 times those earnings. That question is being asked outside the call — on July 16, 2026, Schwab Network's Tony Bancroft described a company that "posted great earnings" with a stock "pulling back over valuation concerns," and MarketWatch headlined the day "GE boosts profit outlook, but stock falls as booming order growth cools."

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The demand cut is real, and management told you the pain is deferred, not cancelled.** Q1 2026: departures guidance cut from mid-single-digit growth to flat-to-low-single-digit, Middle East down low double digits for the year. Culp's own framing — services "will likely lag changes in air traffic demand by several quarters" — dates the arrival of that hit to roughly **2027**, which is outside every number management has yet guided. The bull case and the bear case are not in conflict about the facts here; they are in conflict about how far out you have to look before it matters.

🔴 **The company cannot ship what it sells, and the gap is widening.** Spare parts delinquency was "up over 2x year-over-year" (Q1 2025) and "up roughly 70% since 2024" (Q1 2026). Management sells this as demand strength ("more than 95% of spare parts revenue already in backlog"). It is also a customer-satisfaction deficit that a competitor with capacity would exploit — and Culp conceded in Q3 2025 that "we know our customers need more from us."

🔴 **Insiders are selling, not buying.** Zero open-market purchases against six sales totalling 38,198 shares. Not damning on its own; entirely consistent with a management team that believes in the business and thinks the stock is fully priced.

🔴 **Order growth decelerated hard and the market noticed.** Orders were up 87% in Q1 2026 (an unrepeatable comparison) and up 17% in Q2 2026. The arithmetic is innocent; the reaction — a roughly 4% drop on a beat-and-raise, the second consecutive negative print reaction per MarketWatch — is the signal.

🔴 **Boeing is publicly questioning GE's delivery reliability.** On July 16, 2026, Reuters reported Culp "pushed back... against concerns raised by Boeing that GEnx engine delivery delays could hold up the planemaker's 787 production ramp-up." When your largest airframe customer starts naming you in public as its constraint, the supply-chain story is not finished.

Engine selection is a 30-year decision.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from "constraint" to "delinquency."** In 2025 the problem was described in terms of inputs GE was waiting on. By 2026 the same problem is described in terms of shipments customers are waiting on. The bottleneck did not disappear — it moved downstream to where the customer feels it. That is progress *and* an admission.

**Culp pre-loaded the global-financial-crisis analogy before he needed it.** The Q1 2026 line about services lagging traffic by several quarters "to be followed by a period of above-average growth" is a two-part construction, and only the second half is comforting. He is telling you, in advance and on the record, that a soft patch is coming and that he wants you to hold through it. Management that pre-frames a future air-pocket is being straight with you; it is also telling you the air-pocket exists.

**The de-risking language in Q1 2026 is unusually specific and worth trusting.** "Approximately two thirds of the engines due for our projected shop visits for all of 2026 are currently off wing, either in our shops or waiting to be inducted," and "our pipeline of planned engine removals in the second and third quarters combined with engines that are currently off wing exceeds our shop visit guide." That is a company showing you its inventory of future revenue. It is why the 2026 guide is safe. **It is also why 2026 tells you nothing about 2027** — the engines that will be in the shop next year are the ones flying today, on routes whose economics just changed.

**The organisational consolidation reads as a company shifting from fixing to harvesting.** Q4 2025: the Technology & Operations team, created only a year earlier to break supply constraints, was folded into Commercial Engines & Services under Mohammad Ali; customer-facing teams under Jason Tonich moved to report directly to Culp; Russell Stokes, a 29-year veteran and "one of the first leaders I met here at GE," announced his retirement for July 2026. You stand up a crisis organisation when you have a crisis and you dissolve it into the line when you don't. Read that as confirmation the supply emergency is over — and as a reminder that the easy operational gains have now been taken.

**Capital allocation is conspicuously not discussed.** Across five calls there is extensive discussion of investing roughly $1 billion a year in US manufacturing, ~$3 billion a year in R&D, ~$500 million into LEAP maintenance capacity, and $300 million into a Singapore repair facility — and essentially no discussion of buybacks or the dividend, despite $8–9 billion of annual free cash flow. Management is reinvesting into the ramp. That is the right call operationally. It also means **shareholders are not being handed a mechanical support under the stock**, which matters at 45 times earnings.

**Two questions were answered by the CFO that you would expect the CEO to take** (the defence-acquisition-reform question in Q1 2025, the customer-segment-risk question in Q1 2026). Minor, and I read nothing sinister into it.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** There is no honest way to read these five transcripts against these financials and conclude otherwise. Revenue is compounding at 16% over three years, operating profit went from $8.4 billion to a guided $10.6 billion in two years, the 2028 margin target was hit in 2025, the supply chain that was the whole bear case in early 2025 is visibly repaired, and the guidance record is 8-for-8 with two raises inside six months. Management has been specific, has been conservative, and has delivered above its own conservatism every time.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position: you are not being asked to judge the business — you are being asked to judge the price, and the two are being conflated by everyone in the market.** Every fact in this dossier says "excellent company." At $345.73 the market capitalisation is $361 billion against $8.9–9.2 billion of guided 2026 free cash flow — roughly **40 times free cash flow, and roughly 45 times the raised earnings guide of $7.65–7.85**. Premium engine and aerospace-systems peers (RTX, Safran, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell) typically trade at 25–35 times free cash flow. GE deserves the top of that band and arguably a touch beyond it. It is trading above the band. The excess is not a mispricing to exploit; it is the market's correct recognition of quality, plus a premium for the fact that this management has beaten every number for eight straight quarters — a premium that, by construction, only pays if they beat the *ninth*, *tenth* and *eleventh* too, into a demand backdrop management itself just downgraded.

Concretely: to justify $345.73 you must believe the aftermarket boom is structural rather than a catch-up, at exactly the moment the two executives who run it declined to size the pent-up component ("a hard question to answer quantitatively") and named it first among three drivers, two of which are temporary.

**ECONOMIC MOAT: WIDE, and widening — switching-costs, reinforced by scale-cost and a duopoly structure.** The mechanism is one of the cleanest in industrials. An airline choosing an engine is making a 25-to-30-year decision; the engine is sold at or below cost and the money is made over decades of mandatory, safety-regulated, single-source maintenance. GE is under wing on three of every four commercial flights, with roughly 80,000 engines in service, powers two thirds of US military combat and helicopter fleets, and shares the narrow-body market with Safran through the CFM joint venture — a duopoly against RTX's Pratt & Whitney. About 70% of revenue is recurring services. The 2026 wins (American, United, Delta, Korean Air, Pegasus, Riyadh Air) are not this year's revenue; they are the 2035–2055 annuity being locked in now.

**Width evidence — read the margins, not the returns.** The scan's 4.0% return on invested capital is an artifact of a post-conglomerate balance sheet and must not be used as moat evidence in either direction. The usable evidence: gross margin 36.8% and stable, net margin 19.0% and best-in-class among peers, operating margin hitting the 2028 target three years early, operating profit growing from $8.4B to a guided $10.6B while the installed base compounds. Rising margins on a growing base is a **WIDENING** moat, not an eroding one. The one caveat, stated fairly: management guides segment margins flat through 2026 on new-engine mix and GE9X losses that peak in 2028 — the widening pauses for two years, then resumes.

**SECULAR THREAT: none.** There is no structural force impairing the terminal value here. Air travel is not being disintermediated; jet propulsion is not being displaced by artificial intelligence; the installed base is contracted, regulated and physically inescapable for 30 years per engine. The CFM56 fleet — the thing a naïve model would call the melting ice cube — is in fact **retiring more slowly than management planned** (1.6% versus 2–3%) with two thirds of it not yet through a second shop visit. Open-fan and hybrid-electric architectures are threats GE is itself developing, not threats to GE. The risks in this name are cyclical (air traffic, jet fuel, a Middle East conflict) and valuation-driven. Neither is secular.

**Therefore, the cheapness question does not arise — and that is the finding.** This is not a fear-print to buy, and it is not a value trap to avoid. It is the third thing: **a genuinely wide-moat, structurally sound, superbly-run franchise trading above the range its own quality justifies, with an eight-quarter beat streak fully capitalised into the price and a demand downgrade whose effects management has explicitly deferred into 2027.** The correct action is to know exactly what you would pay and wait for the market to offer it — which, on the evidence of two consecutive negative reactions to good news, it may eventually do.

# Forensic Dossier — GE Aerospace (GE)

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has moved through three distinct phases in five quarters, and the direction of travel is unambiguously upward — which is precisely why the setup deserves scrutiny.

**Phase one — "we are supply-constrained, please be patient" (Q1 2025).** The opening call is defensive in structure even though the numbers were good. Larry Culp led with tariffs ("we expect to reduce the tariff costs to roughly $500 million"), with a cautious cut to the departures assumption ("we're taking a more cautious approach and embedding a slower second half"), and with an admission that revenue was being held back by the company's own supply chain: "our spare parts delinquency continues to increase, unfortunately, up over 2x year-over-year," and "total engine units were down 6% with LEAP down 13%." The hero of the story was FLIGHT DECK, the company's in-house lean operating system, and the ask was time.

**Phase two — "the constraint is breaking, and the ceiling is higher than we said" (Q2 2025 through Q4 2025).** At the July 2025 Investor Update the framing flipped from patience to ambition. Management raised the multi-year services outlook by roughly $4 billion versus its March 2024 view — Rahul Ghai: "we went from high single-digit growth expectation to a double-digit growth expectation... coming off a higher starting point" — and introduced a 2028 target of $11.5 billion in operating profit. New drivers were introduced that had not been part of the original spin-off pitch, and they are the most important part of the arc: **fewer CFM56 retirements than modelled** (600 incremental shop visits pulled into the 2028 window because "these fleets are just continuing to fly longer"), **heavier work scopes** on maturing wide-body engines, and **growth of the third-party repair channel**. By Q3 2025 the tone was frankly triumphant — revenue up 26%, defense units up 83%, LEAP delivery growth raised from "15% to 20%" to "more than 20%." By Q4 2025 Culp was able to say the company would hit its $10 billion profit milestone "two years earlier than our outlook has been."

**Phase three — "a macro shock arrived and we are absorbing it" (Q1 2026 to today).** The April 2026 call opens with the Middle East conflict. Departures guidance was cut from mid-single-digit growth to "flat to low single-digit growth," including "a low double-digit decline in the Middle East for the year." But — and this is the pivotal manoeuvre of the whole arc — management simultaneously **held full-year guidance and said it was trending to the high end**, and pre-installed an explanatory framework for why the traffic hit would not show up in the numbers now: "Based on our experience during the global financial crisis, the impact on services will likely lag changes in air traffic demand by several quarters, to be followed by a period of above-average growth."

**Nothing has been quietly dropped.** Every driver introduced has been reaffirmed or raised. That is rare and it is genuinely to management's credit. What has changed is the *nature of the risk*: it moved from an operational problem the company controls (supply chain) to a demand problem it does not (air traffic, jet fuel, geopolitics) — and management's own words locate the arrival of that risk several quarters out, not now.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, then deliberately re-anchored to caution — and the caution is the informative part.**

| Q1 2025 | **Defensive-operational.** Apologetic about output. | "Our spare parts delinquency continues to increase, unfortunately, up over 2x year-over-year." · "Total engine units were down 6% with LEAP down 13%." · "The broader environment is certainly uncertain." |

**The shift from offense to defense is real but narrow.** Management did not become defensive about the *business*; it became defensive about *the tape it cannot control*. Culp's Q1 2026 answer to Seth Seifman on jet fuel is the tell: "I hope what we are taking is a conservative set of assumptions on board here between now and, let us say, Labor Day. Time will tell." That is a CEO buying himself optionality on the second half — and, as of the July 16, 2026 print, it worked exactly as intended.

**Specificity of guidance has gone up, not down**, over the five quarters: from a maintained range in April 2025, to a dated 2028 framework in July 2025, to shop-visit counts (2,300–2,400), retirement percentages (1.6% actual versus 2–3% guided), and durability-kit penetration (">30% of the LEAP-1A installed base") by 2026. Companies in trouble get vaguer. This one got more granular. That is a strong credibility signal.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High.** This is, on the evidence in front of me, one of the more reliable guidance records in large-cap industrials.

Track the promises forward:

1. **Q1 2025 promise:** maintain full-year guidance despite ~$500M of tariff cost and a cut to departures. **Delivered** — Q3 2025 raised guidance "across the board."
2. **Q1 2025 promise:** "15% to 20% growth in LEAP deliveries we expect in 2025." **Over-delivered** — raised to "more than 20%" in Q3 2025; the full year printed LEAP units up 28%, exceeding 1,800, a program record.

**Sandbagging pattern: confirmed, and management effectively admitted it.** Ghai, Q1 2026: "had it not been for the environment that we are in... **we would have raised our guidance**. The first quarter was about $300 million better than what we had expected at the beginning of the year." That is a CFO telling you the number is conservative and holding the beat in reserve. Three months later he spent it.

**The investment consequence of a High score is counter-intuitive.** An 8-for-8 beat rate with serial raises does not create an opportunity — it *removes* one. There is no expectations gap left to arbitrage. The market has learned this management sandbags, and prices the sandbag. That is why the stock fell about 4% on a quarter that beat by 9% and raised the full year by roughly 7% at the midpoint.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The one question management cannot answer, and analysts keep asking: how much of the aftermarket boom is structural versus pent-up?**

Noah Poponak (Goldman Sachs) asked it directly in Q2 2025: "I wonder if you can quantify the duration of the pent-up demand? Will it take you 1, 2, 3 years to get through that?" Culp's answer: **"Well, it's a hard question to answer quantitatively."** He then redirected to the backlog. Scott Mikus (Melius) asked the same thing from the other side in Q3 2025 — "has anything structurally changed about the business model that could cause your aftermarket growth to decouple or sustainably outperform [available-seat-kilometre] growth over the long-term?" — and Ghai's answer named three things, two of which are explicitly temporary: **"It's pent-up demand, work scopes and then growth of external channel."**

This is the load-bearing unanswered question in the entire file. Commercial services revenue grew 39% in Q1 2026 while global departures grew low single digits. That gap is not a permanent feature of physics; it is a catch-up. Management will not size it, because sizing it would let the market model the year it closes.

**The margin question, asked every single quarter, and never fully resolved.** Sheila Kahyaoglu (Jefferies) in Q4 2025: margins at the midpoint "imply margins are flat" — walk me through it. Seth Seifman (JPMorgan) the same call: "the headwinds accumulating from a mix perspective." But **Robert Stallard's (Vertical Research) Q3 2025 durability question** — "how long is it going to take to roll that blade out across the installed base?" — got the answer "it's probably a multiyear effort," and by Q1 2026 the durability kit was on only ">30% of the LEAP-1A installed base." A multi-year fleet retrofit is a multi-year cost and a multi-year customer-goodwill liability.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** the price. Nobody on any of these five calls asked why a business guiding to ~15% earnings growth should trade at ~45 times those earnings. That question is being asked outside the call — on July 16, 2026, Schwab Network's Tony Bancroft described a company that "posted great earnings" with a stock "pulling back over valuation concerns," and MarketWatch headlined the day "GE boosts profit outlook, but stock falls as booming order growth cools."

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The demand cut is real, and management told you the pain is deferred, not cancelled.** Q1 2026: departures guidance cut from mid-single-digit growth to flat-to-low-single-digit, Middle East down low double digits for the year. Culp's own framing — services "will likely lag changes in air traffic demand by several quarters" — dates the arrival of that hit to roughly **2027**, which is outside every number management has yet guided. The bull case and the bear case are not in conflict about the facts here; they are in conflict about how far out you have to look before it matters.

🔴 **The company cannot ship what it sells, and the gap is widening.** Spare parts delinquency was "up over 2x year-over-year" (Q1 2025) and "up roughly 70% since 2024" (Q1 2026). Management sells this as demand strength ("more than 95% of spare parts revenue already in backlog"). 🔴 **Insiders are selling, not buying.** Zero open-market purchases against six sales totalling 38,198 shares. Not damning on its own; entirely consistent with a management team that believes in the business and thinks the stock is fully priced.

🔴 **Order growth decelerated hard and the market noticed.** Orders were up 87% in Q1 2026 (an unrepeatable comparison) and up 17% in Q2 2026. 🔴 **Margin expansion is on hold until 2028 by management's own account.** GE9X losses "should also peak by the time we get to 2028"; Commercial Engines & Services margins guided flat for 2026.

🟢 **The 2028 targets were hit in 2025–2026.** Both the $10 billion profit milestone (two years early) and the ~21% margin target (three years early). Management set a bar and cleared it before the gun went off.

🟢 **The CFM56 tail is longer than anyone modelled, and this is externally verifiable.** Retirements 1.6% in 2025 against a 2–3% guide; shop visits holding 2,300–2,400 through 2028 with "no big decline come 2030"; two thirds of the fleet has not yet had a second shop visit. This company earns roughly its entire net debt load in free cash every single year. Solvency (Altman-Z of 3.7) is a non-issue.

🟢 **The competitive position on new platforms is being extended, not defended.** Q1 2026 alone: American committed to 300+ LEAP-1A engines with options for 200 more; United selected 300 GE9X engines, making it the largest GE9X operator globally; Delta committed to 60 GE9X with options for 60 more. Engine selection is a 30-year decision.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from "constraint" to "delinquency."** In 2025 the problem was described in terms of inputs GE was waiting on. By 2026 the same problem is described in terms of shipments customers are waiting on. The bottleneck did not disappear — it moved downstream to where the customer feels it. That is progress *and* an admission.

**Culp pre-loaded the global-financial-crisis analogy before he needed it.** The Q1 2026 line about services lagging traffic by several quarters "to be followed by a period of above-average growth" is a two-part construction, and only the second half is comforting. He is telling you, in advance and on the record, that a soft patch is coming and that he wants you to hold through it. Management that pre-frames a future air-pocket is being straight with you; it is also telling you the air-pocket exists.

**The de-risking language in Q1 2026 is unusually specific and worth trusting.** "Approximately two thirds of the engines due for our projected shop visits for all of 2026 are currently off wing, either in our shops or waiting to be inducted," and "our pipeline of planned engine removals in the second and third quarters combined with engines that are currently off wing exceeds our shop visit guide." That is a company showing you its inventory of future revenue. It is why the 2026 guide is safe. **It is also why 2026 tells you nothing about 2027** — the engines that will be in the shop next year are the ones flying today, on routes whose economics just changed.

**The organisational consolidation reads as a company shifting from fixing to harvesting.** Q4 2025: the Technology & Operations team, created only a year earlier to break supply constraints, was folded into Commercial Engines & Services under Mohammad Ali; customer-facing teams under Jason Tonich moved to report directly to Culp; Russell Stokes, a 29-year veteran and "one of the first leaders I met here at GE," announced his retirement for July 2026. You stand up a crisis organisation when you have a crisis and you dissolve it into the line when you don't. Read that as confirmation the supply emergency is over — and as a reminder that the easy operational gains have now been taken.

**Capital allocation is conspicuously not discussed.** Across five calls there is extensive discussion of investing roughly $1 billion a year in US manufacturing, ~$3 billion a year in R&D, ~$500 million into LEAP maintenance capacity, and $300 million into a Singapore repair facility — and essentially no discussion of buybacks or the dividend, despite $8–9 billion of annual free cash flow. Management is reinvesting into the ramp. That is the right call operationally. It also means **shareholders are not being handed a mechanical support under the stock**, which matters at 45 times earnings.

**Two questions were answered by the CFO that you would expect the CEO to take** (the defence-acquisition-reform question in Q1 2025, the customer-segment-risk question in Q1 2026). Minor, and I read nothing sinister into it.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** There is no honest way to read these five transcripts against these financials and conclude otherwise. Revenue is compounding at 16% over three years, operating profit went from $8.4 billion to a guided $10.6 billion in two years, the 2028 margin target was hit in 2025, the supply chain that was the whole bear case in early 2025 is visibly repaired, and the guidance record is 8-for-8 with two raises inside six months. Management has been specific, has been conservative, and has delivered above its own conservatism every time.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position: you are not being asked to judge the business — you are being asked to judge the price, and the two are being conflated by everyone in the market.** Every fact in this dossier says "excellent company." At $345.73 the market capitalisation is $361 billion against $8.9–9.2 billion of guided 2026 free cash flow — roughly **40 times free cash flow, and roughly 45 times the raised earnings guide of $7.65–7.85**. Premium engine and aerospace-systems peers (RTX, Safran, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell) typically trade at 25–35 times free cash flow. GE deserves the top of that band and arguably a touch beyond it. It is trading above the band. The excess is not a mispricing to exploit; it is the market's correct recognition of quality, plus a premium for the fact that this management has beaten every number for eight straight quarters — a premium that, by construction, only pays if they beat the *ninth*, *tenth* and *eleventh* too, into a demand backdrop management itself just downgraded.

Concretely: to justify $345.73 you must believe the aftermarket boom is structural rather than a catch-up, at exactly the moment the two executives who run it declined to size the pent-up component ("a hard question to answer quantitatively") and named it first among three drivers, two of which are temporary.

**ECONOMIC MOAT: WIDE, and widening — switching-costs, reinforced by scale-cost and a duopoly structure.** The mechanism is one of the cleanest in industrials. An airline choosing an engine is making a 25-to-30-year decision; the engine is sold at or below cost and the money is made over decades of mandatory, safety-regulated, single-source maintenance. GE is under wing on three of every four commercial flights, with roughly 80,000 engines in service, powers two thirds of US military combat and helicopter fleets, and shares the narrow-body market with Safran through the CFM joint venture — a duopoly against RTX's Pratt & Whitney. About 70% of revenue is recurring services. The 2026 wins (American, United, Delta, Korean Air, Pegasus, Riyadh Air) are not this year's revenue; they are the 2035–2055 annuity being locked in now.

**Width evidence — read the margins, not the returns.** The scan's 4.0% return on invested capital is an artifact of a post-conglomerate balance sheet and must not be used as moat evidence in either direction. The usable evidence: gross margin 36.8% and stable, net margin 19.0% and best-in-class among peers, operating margin hitting the 2028 target three years early, operating profit growing from $8.4B to a guided $10.6B while the installed base compounds. Rising margins on a growing base is a **WIDENING** moat, not an eroding one. The one caveat, stated fairly: management guides segment margins flat through 2026 on new-engine mix and GE9X losses that peak in 2028 — the widening pauses for two years, then resumes.

**SECULAR THREAT: none.** There is no structural force impairing the terminal value here. Air travel is not being disintermediated; jet propulsion is not being displaced by artificial intelligence; the installed base is contracted, regulated and physically inescapable for 30 years per engine. The CFM56 fleet — the thing a naïve model would call the melting ice cube — is in fact **retiring more slowly than management planned** (1.6% versus 2–3%) with two thirds of it not yet through a second shop visit. Open-fan and hybrid-electric architectures are threats GE is itself developing, not threats to GE. The risks in this name are cyclical (air traffic, jet fuel, a Middle East conflict) and valuation-driven. Neither is secular.

**Therefore, the cheapness question does not arise — and that is the finding.** This is not a fear-print to buy, and it is not a value trap to avoid. It is the third thing: **a genuinely wide-moat, structurally sound, superbly-run franchise trading above the range its own quality justifies, with an eight-quarter beat streak fully capitalised into the price and a demand downgrade whose effects management has explicitly deferred into 2027.** The correct action is to know exactly what you would pay and wait for the market to offer it — which, on the evidence of two consecutive negative reactions to good news, it may eventually do.
